# RustyNES v2.6.13 "Slack"

The cartridge outgrows the die, and three consumers want the same bus.

An SDR SDRAM controller, a behavioural part model, a four-way arbiter and a console bridge, all written from the AS4C32M16SB-7 datasheet revision 1.4. No third-party controller was read; ADR 0037 applies.

**The emulation core is unchanged.** No chip crate changes, so AccuracyCoin 141/141 (RAM decoder) and nestest 0-diff hold by construction, and were re-run anyway.

## The budget was never one number

v2.6.12's cartridge was fitted at 468 of 553 M10K blocks against a mapper scope whose worst case is 768 KiB, so the memory has to leave the die. The question is how much latency the console tolerates, and the previous step answered it with a single figure read off the fetch structure and never measured.

`nes_top` gains `CHR_LAT`, a pipeline that is the identity at zero and asks the console directly: delay the byte until a gate fails. Three consumers, three answers:

| consumer | lead | budget | measured | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| background and sprite fetch | 7 master clocks | 28 cycles | 17 | met |
| the `$2007` data port | 2 master clocks | 8 cycles | -- | met by handshake |
| the CPU, sampling at mc7 | 7 master clocks | 24 cycles | 28 | short by 4 |

Four cycles of every budget go to the console-domain crossing, and that is not optional: the flat address is a runtime modulo computed in a 46.6 ns domain, and publishing it combinationally into an 11.64 ns one costs -24.769 ns of setup.

The fetch fits. The `$2007` port could never fit -- half its budget is the crossing -- so it does not go over the shared bus at all: `ppu2c02` gains a `BUFFER_HANDSHAKE` parameter, asks through a port of its own on the arbiter, and fills its read buffer when the byte arrives, which it can afford because the CPU does not read that buffer until its next `$2007` access. The shared address bus is untouched, so the ALE and hybrid-address ROMs still see the composed {v high, octal latch} exactly as before.

The CPU's 28 is measured under the console's densest pattern -- a CHR fetch every two dots and a PRG read every CPU cycle -- and no gate in the ladder reaches that pattern: off the die the console passes **142 of 142**, every gate the on-die build passes. But the margin is one cycle wide, measured directly (below), so the shortfall is a real property of on-demand arbitration rather than an artefact of the synthetic stimulus. The arbiter gate asserts it rather than noting it, so the day the path meets the deadline the gate fails and says so.

## The defect only a banked cartridge could see

The `$2007` handshake shipped carrying the **raw** fourteen bits the PPU presents, with the CHR region base added. For NROM that is right by coincidence, because the mapper's translation is the identity there -- which is why `ppu-misc-2007-stress` passed off-die throughout, and why the defect landed inside the same change that fixed the port's latency.

The two CNROM gates could see it. The oracle reads `$01`, `$01`, `$02` from `$2007` at cycles 61, 85 and 89; the DUT read `$00` every time, because every banked-CHR board was reading bank zero.

The fix removes the address rather than correcting it. `cart.sv` already publishes the mapper's translation for the fetch path, so the `$2007` request now carries no address at all and the bridge takes that same value -- one source of truth for where CHR lives, instead of two that agree only on NROM. It is captured six cycles after the request rather than on its edge, because that translation is registered on the console clock, a quarter the rate of the SDRAM one, and on the edge it still holds the previous dot's fetch address.

**A one-cycle margin, found by nearly deleting the thing that provided it.** The request is held twice: six cycles for the address, then until the cycle after the CPU's own PRG read is answered -- the widest gap a CPU cycle has. The second wait was built for the PRG mismatch beside the wrong byte, and once the address was fixed a control that issued at a flat +7 with no deferral passed both CNROM gates, which read as the deferral buying nothing. It was removed. The deployed code then issued at +6, and both gates failed again. The control and the code differed by one cycle -- so the CPU's deadline off the die is thin enough that a single cycle of another requester's placement decides it, which is the concrete argument for scheduling the bus rather than arbitrating it.

## One binary, two labels

`USE_SDRAM` reaches Verilator as a `-G` parameter rather than as a file, so switching it changes what the binary is while leaving every prerequisite older than the target. Make reports the target up to date, and the next suite runs the previous configuration's build under the new configuration's name.

It happened here. An off-die ladder followed by an on-die one, with nothing edited between them, produced two logs from one binary -- and the second was labelled on-die while being the off-die build. It reproduced the off-die failures exactly, which is what made it convincing and what made it nearly pass as a real result. Earlier pairs escaped by accident: an RTL edit between them made the sources newer.

The build now takes a stamp file named for the value as a prerequisite. Demonstrated by mutation: without it a switch schedules zero rebuilds; with it, one.

## Two latches Verilator cannot see

`ppu2c02`'s handshake assigned two signals only under `BUFFER_HANDSHAKE`, so in the shipped on-die build -- where that parameter is false -- the only assignment either reached was the reset branch. A variable that holds its previous value on every live path is a latch, and Quartus said so twice. Verilator elaborates the same dead branches and has no opinion about what they become in gates, so the lint gate was green throughout. The comment beside them asserted the defect as a virtue: "outside BUFFER_HANDSHAKE neither signal ever moves" -- which is true, and is exactly the condition that infers the latch.

Both `tb/quartus_clean.py` and `tb/check_warnings.py` caught it independently, the second by the warning **set** rather than a count.

## The open row

Accesses no longer auto-precharge. A row is opened and left open, so a second access to the same row skips both the precharge and the activate: a hit costs 6 cycles where a miss costs 10, and the worst background fetch falls from 16 to 14. tRAS's 120 us **maximum** is respected by an early close in idle -- a row left open indefinitely is a data-loss defect the datasheet states and no functional gate can see.

Two defects came out of the rewrite. Re-entering the idle state while the request was still asserted issued every access **twice**; a flag cleared on the request falling never clears when requests are back to back, so the fix is a one-cycle acknowledge state rather than a flag. And subtracting one from CAS the way the other waits are computed broke every read to `0x0000` -- CAS is "data appears at cycle N", not a command-to-command gap, a different shape from tRCD, tRP and tRFC. The behavioural model was silent about it; the round trip through the arbiter gate is what caught it.

## Two MiSTer tickets close

- **`sdram_sz` is consumed, validity bit first.** The word powers up as `0x0000`,
and "the HPS has not answered yet" is a different fact from "there is no board", so `absent` is deliberately not `!present`: both are false while the answer is unknown, and no access is granted against memory nothing has confirmed exists. The gate is exhaustive over all 65,536 values.
- **`status_menumask` is computed rather than tied off.** The Reset entry is
greyed out whenever the console is already held in reset, because a menu entry that does nothing when selected reads as a working feature.

## What ships

**The console still runs from the die**, and that is a choice rather than a limitation: off the die it passes the entire ladder, 142 of 142, with better timing margin and 384 fewer M10K blocks. The reason is that an off-die core cannot run at all without the SDRAM add-on, so shipping it would make the core unusable on a bare DE10-Nano that the on-die build serves today, in exchange for headroom nothing yet needs -- rung 7's five mapper families fit on the die at 468 of 553 blocks. The bitstream here is the on-die configuration, unchanged in behaviour and now free of the two inferred latches. The flip belongs to the release where a board actually needs the space, and it will need a fallback for a missing one.

## The build

Quartus Prime Lite 17.0.2 Build 602, device 5CSEBA6U23I7, fitter seed 3.

| | |
|---|---|
| errors | 0 |
| warnings | 4, matching the pinned manifest exactly; none cites this project's RTL |
| worst setup | **+0.317 ns**, Slow 1100mV -40C |
| worst hold | **+0.068 ns**, Slow 1100mV -40C |
| corners checked | all four; the binding one is discovered by pattern, not assumed |
| artifact | `releases/RustyNES_MiSTer-v2.6.13.rbf`, md5 `2c2fa6eb0f751b2c9b60fcf903f2bf3f` |

It supersedes `RustyNES_MiSTer-v2.6.12.rbf`, and only by being newer: no defect is known in that bitstream. The two inferred latches this release removes were in the on-die build, and a latch on a signal nothing reads changes no behaviour -- it is a synthesis-quality defect, and a warning that had to stop being emitted before the warning **set** could be pinned.

## What no gate here reaches

**No hardware has run this bitstream.** A booting core, a synced display, audible audio and a working controller are not claimed. The palette, the video timing constants, the audio's absolute level and its band-limiting sit downstream of every gate by construction -- the PPU gate compares the pre-palette index and the APU gate per-channel integer levels -- and the SDRAM part itself is a behavioural model written from the datasheet, not silicon.
